title: Linked List Cycle Detection
directAnswer: Run two pointers from the head: slow moves one node per step, fast moves two. If there's a cycle, fast eventually laps slow and they meet — return true. If fast reaches null, the list ends, so there's no cycle — return false. This is Floyd's Tortoise and Hare: O(n) time, O(1) space. A hash set of visited nodes also works but costs O(n) space.

remember.formula:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow is fast: return True
return False
rules: Check `fast` **and** `fast.next` before moving — fast advances two, so both must be non-null to avoid a NullPointerException.
Compare the two pointers by **identity** (`is` / `==` on references), never by value — different nodes can share a value.
If `fast` (or `fast.next`) hits null, the list terminates, so there's definitively no cycle.
Inside a cycle the gap between fast and slow shrinks by one each step, so they are guaranteed to collide — they can never 'jump over' each other.
For the *start* of the cycle (LeetCode 142): after they meet, reset one pointer to head and advance both by one until they meet again.
whenToUse: Detect whether a linked list (or implicit 'next' function) loops back on itself
Constant-space cycle detection where a hash set is too memory-hungry
Find a duplicate via index-chasing (Find the Duplicate Number) or cycle entry (Linked List Cycle II)
Happy Number and other 'follow next repeatedly, does it loop?' problems
antiSignals: You also need the set of all visited nodes for something else → a hash set is more useful
Nodes are not uniquely addressable / you only have values → identity comparison won't work, rethink
You need the cycle length or entry immediately → still Floyd's, but with the extra second phase
remember.takeaway: Two pointers at different speeds turn cycle detection from an O(n)-space bookkeeping problem into an O(1)-space race. The same tortoise-and-hare idea reappears in Linked List Cycle II, Find the Duplicate Number, and Happy Number.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know the O(1)-space fast/slow trick instead of defaulting to a hash set, and whether you guard the fast pointer's two-step advance against null.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Dereferencing fast.next.next without checking fast and fast.next first, or comparing node values instead of node identity.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the hash-set baseline, then upgrade to Floyd's for O(1) space. Explain *why* they must meet (the gap shrinks by one each step) and mention the cycle-entry extension.

problemStatement:
Given `head`, the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it.

There is a cycle if some node can be reached again by continuously following the `next` pointer. Return `true` if there is a cycle, otherwise return `false`. You should not modify the list.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10⁴]
The cycle, if present, is created by the tail's next pointing to an earlier node (or to itself)
understanding: We only answer yes/no: does following next forever loop, or does it terminate at null? We don't return the cycle's location here (that's LeetCode 142). A node's next pointing back to any earlier node — including itself — counts as a cycle.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a node's next point to itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a single node whose next is itself is a valid one-node cycle and must return true.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to modify the list (e.g. mark visited nodes)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll treat the list as read-only. Floyd's needs no mutation; marking nodes would corrupt the input and is fragile.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you also need where the cycle begins?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not for this problem — just true/false. If you did, I'd add Floyd's phase two: reset one pointer to head and walk both one step at a time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about the empty list or a single node with no cycle?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Empty list and a lone node with next = null both return false; the while-loop guard handles them without special-casing.

examples.explanation: The tail node -4 points back to node 2, forming a cycle 2 → 0 → -4 → 2.
The tail node 2 points back to the head, so the two nodes cycle forever.
A single node whose next is null terminates — no cycle.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Floyd's fast/slow is the default for O(1) space; reach for a hash set only if you need the visited nodes anyway.

approaches.name: Hash Set — Remember Visited Nodes
approaches.whenToMention: State it first as the intuitive baseline, then offer Floyd's to save the O(n) space.
hints: If you walk the list and keep a record of every node you've already stepped on, what does it mean to arrive at a node that's already in your record?
Store node references (not values) in a hash set. Before moving on, check whether the current node is already in the set.
If the current node is already present, you've looped back — return true. If you walk off the end into null, return false.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited at most once and triggers O(1) average set operations → O(n) time. The set can hold up to n node references → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the list one node at a time, recording each node you visit in a hash set of node references. If you ever reach a node that's already in the set, you must have followed `next` back to somewhere you've been — that's a cycle.

**Why store node references, not values.** Two different nodes can hold the same `val` (the list `[1, 1]` with no cycle is perfectly legal). Hashing on identity — the object reference in Java, `id()`-style identity via the object itself in Python — guarantees we only flag a true revisit, not a coincidental value match.

**Why it terminates.** A finite list with no cycle ends at `null`, so the loop exits and we return `false`. A list with a cycle has no `null`, but it has only finitely many distinct nodes, so within n steps we are forced to land on one we've already stored.

**Why we still prefer Floyd's.** This is correct and easy to explain, but it spends O(n) memory to remember every node. The fast/slow pointer method gets the same answer in O(1) space, which is what an interviewer is usually fishing for once you've shown the baseline.
approaches.insight: This is the generic 'have I been here before?' membership trick applied to nodes. It's the honest first answer, and naming its O(n) space cost is exactly what motivates the jump to Floyd's.

dryRun.intro: We add each node to the set as we visit it and stop when we revisit one.

java.explanation: Stores node references — identity, not value — so coincidental equal values don't false-trigger.
add returns false when the node is already present, i.e. we've looped back.
Advance one node; if curr becomes null the list terminated with no cycle.

python.explanation: Membership test by object identity — a revisited node means a cycle.
Record the node so future steps can detect a return to it.
Reached null without revisiting — no cycle.

pitfalls: Storing values instead of node references — [1, 1] with no cycle would falsely report true.
Forgetting the null check in the loop guard and dereferencing past the tail.
Accepting the O(n) space when an O(1) solution exists — say it's a baseline, not the final answer.

approaches.name: Floyd's Tortoise & Hare — Fast/Slow Pointers (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'a fast runner laps a slow runner on a circular track'.
hints: Picture two runners on a track. If the track is a straight line, the faster runner just reaches the end. What happens on a circular track?
Start slow and fast at the head. Each step move slow by one and fast by two. If they ever point at the same node, there's a cycle.
Guard the fast pointer: only continue while fast and fast.next are non-null, because fast dereferences two links per step. If fast falls off the end, return false.
approaches.complexityReasoning: No cycle → fast reaches the end in n/2 steps. With a cycle → once both are inside the loop, the gap closes by one per step, so they meet within at most the cycle length. Total work is O(n); only two pointers are stored, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Two pointers leave the head together; `slow` takes single steps, `fast` takes double steps. On a straight (acyclic) list `fast` simply runs off the end. On a cyclic list `fast` is condemned to loop forever and will inevitably catch up to `slow` from behind.

**Why they are guaranteed to meet.** Once both pointers are inside the cycle, consider the distance from `fast` to `slow` measured *forward around the loop*. Every step, `slow` gains 1 and `fast` gains 2, so that gap shrinks by exactly 1 each step. A quantity that decreases by 1 each step (modulo the cycle length) must eventually hit 0 — meaning they land on the same node. Crucially, because the gap changes by 1, fast can never 'leap over' slow without first matching it.

**Why the loop guard is `fast != null && fast.next != null`.** `fast` reads `fast.next.next` each iteration. If `fast` is null we'd crash on `fast.next`; if `fast.next` is null we'd crash on the second hop. Both conditions being true is exactly what guarantees the double step is safe — and either being false means we hit the end of an acyclic list, so we return false.

**Why identity comparison.** We test `slow == fast` on the node *references*. Comparing `slow.val == fast.val` is a classic bug: distinct nodes routinely share values, which would report phantom cycles.

**Memory win.** We replaced the hash set's O(n) bookkeeping with two integer-sized pointers. Same O(n) time, but O(1) space — the upgrade interviewers are listening for.
approaches.insight: Differing speeds convert 'is there a loop?' into 'does the hare lap the tortoise?'. The gap-shrinks-by-one argument is the whole proof, and it generalises: reset one pointer to the head after they meet and you get the cycle's entry node (Linked List Cycle II) for free.

dryRun.intro: slow steps once, fast steps twice. They are compared after each move.

java.explanation: Tortoise — advances one node per iteration.
Both must be non-null because fast hops two links; failing this means the list ended (no cycle).
Hare — advances two nodes, so it catches slow from behind inside any cycle.
Reference equality: same node means the hare lapped the tortoise → cycle.

python.explanation: Both pointers start at the head.
Guard the two-step hop; if either is None the list terminates.
Move twice as fast as slow.
Identity check (is), not value — distinct nodes can share a value.

edgeCases.behavior: fast is null on entry, the loop never runs, returns false.
fast and fast.next are non-null; after one step slow=1, fast=1 → returns true.
After one step fast = null, loop guard fails, returns false.

pitfalls: Writing fast.next.next without the fast && fast.next guard — null dereference on acyclic lists.
Comparing slow.val == fast.val instead of the references — false positives on repeated values.
Starting fast at head.next as a 'micro-optimization' then mishandling the off-by-one in the meeting condition.

commonMistakes: Calling fast.next.next without first checking fast and fast.next are non-null.
Comparing node values instead of node identity to detect the meeting point.
Defaulting to the O(n) hash set when O(1) Floyd's is the intended answer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unguarded two-step advance
commonMistakesDetailed.why: fast hops two links per iteration, so both fast and fast.next must be non-null. Skipping the guard throws on any list that ends.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing values instead of identity
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Different nodes can carry equal values, so a value match does not imply the same node. Use reference/identity comparison.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if slow is fast:
    return True

followupVariations.title: Linked List Cycle II
followupVariations.hint: Return the node where the cycle begins: after they meet, reset one pointer to head and step both by one until they meet again.

followupVariations.title: Find the Duplicate Number
followupVariations.hint: Treat the array as a linked list where i → nums[i]; the duplicate is the cycle entry found via Floyd's.

followupVariations.title: Happy Number
followupVariations.hint: Follow the digit-square-sum function with slow/fast; a non-happy number falls into a cycle.

patternNote: Floyd's fast/slow pointers. The go-to whenever you must detect or locate a cycle in O(1) space — on real linked lists (Cycle / Cycle II) or implicit ones defined by a next-function (Find the Duplicate Number, Happy Number).
